terms.grammar: phrase: gerō with the reflexive, and an adverb or a clause of manner
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.90: quantō superiōrēs sīmus, tantō nōs gerāmus summissius
Cic. Fam. 11.27.5: quōnam modō gererem mē adversus Caesarem
terms.comment: Latin says how someone behaved with a verb and an adverb where English uses the noun: optimē sē gessit, his behaviour was excellent. Lewis & Short: “to bear, deport, behave, or conduct one’s self”.

evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.3.7: ā quō mōrēs prīmum mox ēloquentiam discat
Hor. Ars 156: aetātis cujusque notandī sunt tibi mōrēs
terms.comment: The plural of mōs, custom (see practice): a person’s habitual behaviour and character, good or bad. Lewis & Short: “conduct, behavior; in plur., manners, morals, character”.

phrases.latin: rēctē praecipere videantur, quī monent, ut, quantō superiōrēs sīmus, tantō nōs gerāmus summissius
phrases.english: those seem to give good advice who warn us that the higher we stand, the more humbly we should behave

phrases.latin: ā quō mōrēs prīmum mox ēloquentiam discat, quae male sine mōribus discitur
phrases.english: from whom he may learn good conduct first, then eloquence, which is badly learned without it

phrases.latin: in maximīs rēbus quōnam modō gererem mē adversus Caesarem, ūsus tuō cōnsiliō sum
phrases.english: in matters of the greatest moment I took your advice on how I should behave towards Caesar
